title: Barracoon: The Story of the Last Black Cargo
author: Zora Neale Hurston
target_audience: Readers interested in African American history
Students and scholars of slavery and the African diaspora
Fans of Zora Neale Hurston’s literary works
Those interested in oral history and anthropology
General readers seeking vivid historical narratives
core_themes: The transatlantic slave trade and its human cost
The resilience and humanity of the enslaved
The process and power of oral history
The legacy of slavery in the United States
primary_purpose: To preserve and share the firsthand account of Cudjo Lewis, the last known survivor of the transatlantic slave trade, offering a rare, personal perspective on the horrors of enslavement, Middle Passage, and life in America post-Emancipation.

structure_format.organization: Chronological, centered on Cudjo Lewis’s life from pre-capture Africa, through enslavement, to his life in Alabama
features: Transcribed dialect capturing Cudjo’s authentic voice
Historical context and editorial framing by Zora Neale Hurston
Photographs and supporting materials in published edition

key_concepts_lessons: The slave trade’s devastating impact on African societies and individuals.
Cultural identity and memory are preserved through storytelling and oral history.
The Middle Passage was an ordeal of extraordinary suffering and trauma.
The legacy of slavery shapes family, community, and personal identity long after emancipation.
Listening to primary sources is critical for an unfiltered understanding of history.
notable_features: Based on extensive interviews with Cudjo Lewis in his own words
Preserved African American Vernacular English and authentic dialect
Offers a rare primary account of the last generation of enslaved Africans
Suppressed for decades; publication delayed until 2018
Blends literature, anthropology, and oral history
cultural_historical_context: Written during the Harlem Renaissance by Zora Neale Hurston, an influential Black author and trained anthropologist. Shelved for decades due to the use of dialect and its frank depiction of Black complicity in the slave trade, the book was first published in 2018, making a significant contribution to the understanding of American slavery and Black history.
reception_impact: Acclaimed as a landmark in American history and literature upon its publication
Praised for restoring Cudjo Lewis’s story and Hurston’s anthropological skill to public awareness
Contributed to public conversations about the legacy of slavery and the importance of first-person narratives
Recognized for the ethical challenges and strengths of using dialect to preserve voice and authenticity
Used as a source in academic and general studies of slavery and oral history
